READING

**Financial arithmetic at face value**

The headline numbers frame this as a £950,000 question: VELLACOTT costs £2,680,000 net against TARNSIDE's £1,730,000, a gap of £950,000. The fuel saving of £190,000 a year repays that gap in five years. Everything after year five is pure gain on the operating account, and a 2017-built vessel bought in 2026 ought to be in service through the late 2040s at minimum — so the compounding runs for two to three decades, not five years.

To make TARNSIDE the better financial choice you would need either (a) the insurance uplift on the Suilvenaig to be very large, (b) the fuel-price differential to collapse, or (c) the Suilvenaig to have a materially shorter remaining life than the re-engined Brindlemere. None of those is obviously true. A 2017 hull should have lower maintenance and insurance costs than a 1995 hull even with new engines, not higher ones, and fuel is unlikely to become cheaper over the planning horizon.

**What the £610,000 sale figure actually does**

Kittiwake's valuation is held until 2027-02-11. If VELLACOTT is chosen, handover is 2026-11-20, leaving roughly eleven weeks to sell the Brindlemere within the guaranteed valuation window. That is tight but workable: the vessel is operational (engines have life until end of summer 2027), was hull-surveyed clean in March, and has a known maintenance record with Hebridean & Vaile since 2004. A buyer exists at that price or Kittiwake would not have given the figure. The risk of missing the window is real but not severe — even at a modest discount the net cost comparison still favours VELLACOTT.

**The yard period and charter**

Twelve weeks starting 2027-01-05 falls in the low-frequency winter schedule (five crossings a day), which is the best possible timing. The charter is agreed in principle, not contracted. That distinction matters: "in principle" leaves open price, vessel suitability, and Sorrelbank's availability if another operator wants the same window. TARNSIDE carries execution risk on the charter that tends to be invisible because the cost is already in the headline figure. The £310,000 is also a true cash burn with no residual value.

**The masters problem — serious but bounded**

Losing two of nine masters is the sharpest practical complication of VELLACOTT. A rota of seven for a year-round, single-vessel, eleven-crossing summer service is workable but carries less slack than nine. The more pressing issue is that all seven remaining masters need a six-week endorsement that none currently holds. The Suilvenaig handover is 2026-11-20 — approximately twelve weeks away. The six-week course can in principle begin before handover if enrolment is arranged now, and the November-to-April low-season period (five crossings daily) is precisely the window in which to rotate masters through training without crippling the rota. This requires active management and probably some overlap scheduling, but it is a solvable logistics problem rather than a structural blocker.

If at any point VELLACOTT is chosen, the operator should also price whether recruiting one additional master with the appropriate endorsement is feasible, to restore some rota depth. That is a cost not currently in the VELLACOTT figure, but it is modest relative to the £950,000 cost gap.

**The insurance gap**

The broker not yet having quoted on the Suilvenaig is a genuine unknown. It should not remain one: a quote should be obtainable within days and must be in hand before any purchase commitment. A newer, class-maintained 2017 hull generally attracts better hull-and-machinery rates than a 1995 vessel, so an adverse result would be surprising, but the point is that this is confirmable rather than permanently uncertain. The absence of a quote at this stage of evaluation is a process gap, not a signal that bad news is coming. It would, however, be imprudent to sign anything on the Suilvenaig without it.

**The hull age argument**

TARNSIDE puts new mechanical components into a hull that will be thirty-two years old when it leaves the yard. The engines and gearbox are, quite rightly, the surveyor's concern today. In five to ten years the structural, deck, and systems questions on a mid-1990s vessel will intensify, and the operator will revisit a version of this same decision from a weaker starting position — more capital already spent, a lower sale value (if any), and an older crew roster. The Suilvenaig at nine years old in 2026 is past infant unreliability but nowhere near the phase of accelerating age-related expenditure. The investment case for VELLACOTT is not just five years of fuel payback; it is also the avoidance of the next maintenance decision cycle on a vessel that, post re-engining, would be worth less than the re-engining cost.

**Strategic summary**

TARNSIDE offers certainty: known insurance terms, a full master rota, no linkspan work, and a finite upfront number. Those are real and not trivial. But what it offers is certainty about a vessel whose best years are behind it, at a cost that is recovered slowly and whose benefits plateau early.

VELLACOTT offers a 2017 hull, the same carrying capacity, no winter service disruption, and a fuel saving that repays the cost premium in five years before running for decades more. Its complications — insurance unquoted, masters to train, rota thinned by two — are all resolvable with planning that is available before any commitment is binding.

The balance is not genuinely even. The long-run financial and operational case for the newer vessel is substantially stronger.

---

READING
  The extra £950,000 upfront cost of VELLACOTT is repaid entirely by the annual £190,000 fuel saving within five years. After that the saving compounds for what should be twenty or more years of service from a 2017 hull, while a re-engined 1995 hull would face another expensive decision cycle within that same window. The insurance and masters complications, though real, are resolvable before any binding commitment on the Suilvenaig is made, and neither overturns the long-run arithmetic.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The £950,000 cost premium is recovered through fuel savings alone in five years, leaving two or more decades of a 2017 hull generating net gains that a re-engined 1995 vessel structurally cannot match.
